title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
This incident is an impersonation scam, not a failure of a legitimately deployed AI system. Scammers used AI tools to generate fabricated news content, including a false account of a confrontation between two real, named public figures, and attached that content to promotion of an unlicensed financial platform. The failure is in the production and distribution of synthetic disinformation: AI made it cheap and fast to produce content that carries the surface markers of credible journalism, including names, quotes, and a publication format, without any of the underlying facts.

The deception operates at the consumption stage, where an ordinary reader encounters a professional-looking article and has no built-in mechanism to verify it. Catching it would require either platform-level detection of synthetic content before distribution, or a reader who independently checks the financial services register, searches for corroborating coverage, or already knows the event never happened. ASIC's figures show the scale grew sharply in a short period, which indicates that the barrier to running these schemes is low and falling.

What is not established is who built or operated the specific AI tools used, whether any platform hosting the content was aware of its synthetic origin, and no legal finding has been made against any identified party.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article claiming Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler over an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven never actually occurred. The article was part of an increasingly common scam that uses artificial intelligence to create convincing false content featuring prominent Australians. Australian Securities and Investments Commission research reveals these sophisticated schemes are becoming more prevalent and harder to detect, with scammers building entire fake online ecosystems including fabricated news articles, reviews, and advertisements.

Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams overall, a 182 percent increase from the previous year. The regulator took down 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms, representing respective increases of 279 percent and 151 percent. Alan Kohler ranks among the most commonly impersonated Australians, alongside Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, various politicians, and wealthy figures including Gina Rinehart. ASIC advises consumers to verify financial services licenses and check company details through its free public registers before investing, warning that professional-looking content does not guarantee legitimacy.
